title: Unsupervised Learning
text:
Unsupervised learning is a type of machine learning that aims to discover hidden patterns and structure in data without labeled outcomes. The purpose of performing unsupervised learning on this data is to identify natural groupings of movies and understand whether different types of films follow distinct patterns in terms of budget, cast popularity, and box office performance.
I applied two main unsupervised learning techniques: dimensionality reduction for visualization and clustering for pattern discovery. For dimensionality reduction, I used Principal Component Analysis (PCA) to reduce the feature space while preserving variance. For clustering, I applied K-Means clustering to identify distinct movie archetypes based on their characteristics.
The goal was to determine whether movies naturally group into categories beyond simple genre classifications, and whether these groupings reveal insights about different risk-return profiles in the film industry.
Below is an outline of general information applied to all methods:


In order to be used in unsupervised learning, the data required preprocessing to ensure all features contributed equally to pattern detection.
Feature Selection - I selected numerical features that characterize movie production and performance: budget, revenue, cast popularity, runtime, and ROI. Categorical variables were excluded from clustering since K-Means requires numerical data.
Standardization - The data was scaled using Scikit-learn’s StandardScaler. This z-score standardization is critical for unsupervised learning since clustering algorithms are sensitive to feature magnitudes. Without scaling, budget (in millions) would dominate patterns over features like runtime (in minutes).
Handling Outliers - Extreme outliers were retained since they may represent legitimate movie archetypes (ultra-low-budget breakouts or massive tentpoles) rather than data errors.





Principal Component Analysis (PCA) reduces the dimensionality of data by transforming features into orthogonal principal components that capture maximum variance. PCA identifies linear combinations of original features that explain the most variation in the data.
I applied PCA to visualize the movie dataset in two dimensions while preserving as much information as possible. The first two principal components captured the most important patterns of variation across budget, revenue, cast popularity, and other features.
Purpose: PCA enables visualization of high-dimensional data and can reveal whether movies naturally separate into distinct groups based on their characteristics.



K-Means is a clustering algorithm that partitions data into k distinct groups by minimizing within-cluster variance. The algorithm iteratively assigns data points to clusters and updates cluster centers until convergence.
I applied K-Means clustering to identify natural groupings of movies. The algorithm groups films with similar characteristics (budget levels, cast popularity, revenue performance) into the same cluster.
Model Selection: I used the elbow method and silhouette analysis to determine the optimal number of clusters. The elbow method plots within-cluster sum of squares (WCSS) against k values, looking for the “elbow” where adding more clusters provides diminishing returns. Silhouette analysis measures how well each point fits within its assigned cluster.
Purpose: K-Means reveals whether movies fall into distinct categories with different production strategies and financial outcomes, beyond traditional genre classifications.

Clustering Analysis: Finding Natural Movie Groups
I used K-Means clustering to identify whether movies naturally group into distinct categories based on their characteristics. This reveals market segments like indie films, mid-budget productions, mainstream hits, and blockbusters.

from sklearn.cluster import KMeans

Preparing Features for Clustering
I selected numerical features that capture movie characteristics: budget, revenue, runtime, popularity, and cast popularity. These features were standardized so no single variable dominates the clustering due to scale differences.

# select features for clustering

                   'vote_count', 'cast_popularity', 'roi']

# create feature matrix

# standardize features

title: Unsupervised Learning
text:
Finding Optimal Number of Clusters
I used the elbow method and silhouette scores to determine the best number of clusters. The elbow method plots within-cluster variance against k values, while silhouette scores measure how well each point fits within its assigned cluster.

from sklearn.metrics import silhouette_score

# testing different k values
k_range = range(2, 8)
inertias = []
silhouette_scores = []

for k in k_range:
    kmeans = KMeans(n_clusters=k, random_state=42, n_init=10)
    kmeans.fit(X_scaled)
    inertias.append(kmeans.inertia_)
    silhouette_scores.append(silhouette_score(X_scaled, kmeans.labels_))

# plot results
fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 5))

# elbow plot
ax1.plot(k_range, inertias, 'bo-', linewidth=2, markersize=8)
ax1.set_xlabel('Number of Clusters (k)', fontsize=11, fontweight='bold')
ax1.set_ylabel('Inertia (Within-cluster sum of squares)', fontsize=11, fontweight='bold')
ax1.set_title('Elbow Method', fontsize=13, fontweight='bold')
ax1.grid(True, alpha=0.3)

# silhouette plot
ax2.plot(k_range, silhouette_scores, 'ro-', linewidth=2, markersize=8)
ax2.set_xlabel('Number of Clusters (k)', fontsize=11, fontweight='bold')
ax2.set_ylabel('Silhouette Score', fontsize=11, fontweight='bold')
ax2.set_title('Silhouette Score Method', fontsize=13, fontweight='bold')
ax2.grid(True, alpha=0.3)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

print("\nClustering Metrics:")
print("="*50)
for k, inertia, sil in zip(k_range, inertias, silhouette_scores):
    print(f"k={k}: Inertia={inertia:,.0f}, Silhouette={sil:.3f}")

best_k = k_range[np.argmax(silhouette_scores)]
print(f"\nBest k based on silhouette score: {best_k}")

Performing K-Means Clustering (k=4)

    roi = cluster_summary.loc[i, 'Med_ROI']

title: Unsupervised Learning
text:
Dimensionality Reduction with PCA
With 7 features, visualization becomes difficult. PCA reduces these to 2 principal components that capture the most variance, allowing visualization of the overall movie landscape and how clusters separate.

# perform PCA
pca = PCA(n_components=3)
X_pca = pca.fit_transform(X_scaled)

# explained variance
print("PCA Results:")
print("="*60)
print(f"Component 1 explains {pca.explained_variance_ratio_[0]*100:.1f}% of variance")
print(f"Component 2 explains {pca.explained_variance_ratio_[1]*100:.1f}% of variance")
print(f"Component 3 explains {pca.explained_variance_ratio_[2]*100:.1f}% of variance")
print(f"Total variance explained: {sum(pca.explained_variance_ratio_)*100:.1f}%")

# feature importance for each component
components_df = pd.DataFrame(
    pca.components_.T,
    columns=['PC1', 'PC2', 'PC3'],
    index=cluster_features
)
print("\nFeature Contributions to Principal Components:")
print(components_df.round(3))

# visualize PCA
fig = plt.figure(figsize=(16, 6))

# 2D PCA plot
ax1 = fig.add_subplot(121)
for cluster in [0, 1, 2, 3]:
    mask = df['cluster'] == cluster
    ax1.scatter(X_pca[mask, 0], X_pca[mask, 1], 
               alpha=0.6, s=50, label=labels[cluster], color=colors[cluster])

ax1.set_xlabel(f'PC1 ({pca.explained_variance_ratio_[0]*100:.1f}% variance)', 
              fontsize=11, fontweight='bold')

              fontsize=11, fontweight='bold')

title: Exploratory Data Analysis
text:
Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) is the process of examining and visualizing data to understand its characteristics, identify patterns, and uncover relationships between variables. The purpose of performing EDA on this data is to gain deeper insights into what drives box office success and to prepare the dataset for machine learning modeling.
I conducted univariate, bivariate, and multivariate analyses to examine the cleaned dataset of 2,691 movies. The analysis explored distributions of key variables (budget, revenue, ROI), relationships between features (budget-revenue correlation, genre patterns, seasonal effects), and patterns that inform the prediction task.
The goal was to answer exploratory questions: How does budget relate to revenue? Do certain genres perform better? Does release timing matter? What’s the typical ROI distribution? These insights shaped feature selection and informed expectations for model performance.
Below is an outline of the analytical approach:


The cleaned dataset contains 2,691 movies with 23 features spanning financial metrics, cast information, genre classifications, and temporal characteristics. Key variables include:
Financial Variables: Budget, revenue, ROI, profitability (binary), success category (4-class)
Cast and Production: Cast popularity, production companies, director
Genre and Classification: Primary genre, all genres, budget tier
Temporal Features: Release date, release year, release month, release season
Film Characteristics: Runtime, vote average, vote count, popularity score





I examined the distribution of individual variables to understand their characteristics and identify potential issues.
Numerical Variables: I generated summary statistics (mean, median, standard deviation) and visualized distributions using histograms. This revealed the range and spread of budget, revenue, and ROI values.
Categorical Variables: I calculated frequency counts for genres, budget tiers, and seasons, visualizing them with bar charts to understand category balance.



I analyzed relationships between pairs of variables to identify patterns and correlations.
Budget-Revenue Relationship: I created scatter plots and calculated correlation coefficients to quantify the relationship between production spending and box office earnings.
Genre Performance: I compared success rates across genres using grouped bar charts to identify which categories perform best.
Seasonal Patterns: I analyzed profitability rates by release season to determine whether timing affects outcomes.



I examined interactions between multiple variables simultaneously.
Correlation Matrix: I generated a correlation heatmap showing relationships among all numerical features to identify multicollinearity and feature importance patterns.
Budget Tier Analysis: I compared ROI distributions across budget tiers using box plots to understand how spending level affects returns.

title: Data Cleaning
text:
Data cleaning is the process of identifying and correcting quality issues in raw data to prepare it for analysis. The purpose of performing data cleaning on this dataset is to remove invalid records, handle missing information, and engineer features necessary for machine learning models.
The raw data from TMDB contained 2,812 movies, but several data quality issues made portions unsuitable for analysis. I identified unrealistic financial values, missing cast information, and statistical outliers requiring removal. Beyond addressing quality issues, I engineered five new features that didn’t exist in the raw data but are essential for profitability analysis.
The goal was to transform the raw dataset into a clean, analysis-ready format with complete records and meaningful features. The cleaning process involved validating financial data, filtering problematic records, and creating derived features like ROI, success categories, budget tiers, and seasonal indicators.
Below is an outline of the cleaning approach:


The raw dataset had several problems requiring attention:
Unrealistic Financial Values: Some movies showed budgets under $1 million or revenues under $1,000, likely representing data entry errors or incomplete records.
Statistical Outliers: A handful of records showed ROI values exceeding 100x, representing extreme outliers that would distort analysis.
Missing Information: Some records lacked complete cast or production company information needed for popularity-based analysis.





I created five new features before applying validation filters, ensuring derived metrics were available for filtering criteria.
ROI Calculation: I calculated return on investment by dividing revenue by budget, providing the primary profitability metric.
Binary Profitability: I created a binary indicator marking whether films earned more than they cost.
Success Categories: I classified films into four performance tiers (Bomb, Modest, Hit, Blockbuster) based on ROI thresholds.
Budget Tiers: I grouped films by production budget into four spending categories (Low, Medium, High, Blockbuster) reflecting industry breakpoints.
Release Seasons: I categorized release months into three seasonal periods (Fall, Holiday, Summer) reflecting industry release patterns.



I applied quality thresholds to remove problematic records while maintaining sufficient sample size.
Budget Threshold: Films with budgets below $1 million were excluded as these likely represent incomplete data rather than theatrical releases.
Revenue Threshold: Revenue below $1,000 indicated data quality issues and was filtered out.
ROI Threshold: ROI above 100x represented statistical outliers and was removed.
Completeness Requirement: Records missing cast or production company information were dropped as these features are required for analysis.

text:
Feature Engineering
Before cleaning, I created the key features needed for analysis: ROI and profitability indicators to classify whether movies made money.

# create ROI 
df['roi'] = df['revenue'] / df['budget']

df['profitable'] = (df['revenue'] > df['budget']).astype(int)

# create success categories
def categorize_success(row):
    roi = row['roi']
    if roi < 1:
        return 'Bomb'  # lost money
    elif roi < 2:
        return 'Modest'  # made money but not much
    elif roi < 5:
        return 'Hit'  # strong performer
    else:
        return 'Blockbuster'  # massive success

df['success_category'] = df.apply(categorize_success, axis=1)

# create budget tiers
def categorize_budget(budget):
    if budget < 20_000_000:
        return 'Low'
    elif budget < 80_000_000:
        return 'Medium'
    elif budget < 150_000_000:
        return 'High'
    else:
        return 'Blockbuster'

df['budget_tier'] = df['budget'].apply(categorize_budget)

# create release season
def get_season(month):
    if month in [6, 7, 8]:
        return 'Summer'
    elif month in [11, 12]:
        return 'Holiday'
    elif month in [3, 4, 5]:
        return 'Spring'
    else:
        return 'Fall'

title: Supervised Learning
text:
Supervised learning is a type of machine learning that aims to fit the best model for predicting values of a labeled variable. The purpose of performing supervised learning on this data is to determine whether movie profitability can be predicted using features available before release, and to understand which factors most strongly influence box office success.
I performed binary classification to predict whether films will be profitable (revenue exceeds budget) or unprofitable. Three classification algorithms were trained and compared: Logistic Regression, Random Forest, and Gradient Boosting. The model selection methods, evaluation metrics, and results are discussed in the sections below.
Below is an outline of general information applied to all models:


In order to be used in supervised learning, data must be cleaned, processed, and standardized following specific criteria. The following techniques were performed on the data:
Feature Selection - I selected features available before a film’s release: budget, budget tier, cast popularity, primary genre, release season, release year, and runtime. Post-release metrics like vote average and vote count were excluded since they aren’t available during pre-production when investment decisions get made.
Target Variable - The binary profitable indicator served as the classification target, where 1 indicates revenue exceeded budget and 0 indicates the film lost money.
Handling Categorical Variables - Categorical variables (primary genre, budget tier, release season) were one-hot encoded to be represented as numerical variables and included in the supervised learning models. - What is one-hot encoding?: A machine learning technique that converts categorical data into numerical data, denoted as 0 or 1. The levels of the categorical variable are pivoted so that each level becomes a column. I used 5-fold cross-validation during training to assess model stability and reduce overfitting risk.

Logistic Regression - A linear model that predicts the probability of profitability using a logistic function. It serves as the baseline model and provides interpretable coefficients.

Gradient Boosting - An ensemble method that builds trees sequentially, with each tree correcting errors from previous trees. It often achieves high accuracy but requires careful tuning.

Accuracy - The percentage of correct predictions across all movies.
Precision - The proportion of movies predicted as profitable that actually were profitable. High precision means few false positives.
Recall - The proportion of actually profitable movies that were correctly identified. High recall means few false negatives.
F1-Score - The harmonic mean of precision and recall, balancing both metrics into a single score.
For this application, recall is more important than precision. Studios want to avoid passing on films that would succeed (false negatives) more than they want to avoid greenlighting films that will fail (false positives).

title: Overview
text:
The goal of this data collection phase was to gather comprehensive movie information from The Movie Database (TMDB) to analyze patterns in box office success. TMDB provides detailed financial data, cast information, production details, and temporal features needed for profitability analysis.
I targeted movies with complete budget and revenue information since these financial metrics are essential for the analysis. I only included movies with at least 100 user votes to ensure data quality. I queried the API systematically to retrieve popular films where both production costs and box office earnings are documented.



Predicting box office success has challenged the film industry for decades. Studios invest hundreds of millions in productions with limited ability to forecast performance. Executives rely on star power, comparable film analysis, and gut instinct, but data-driven approaches may reveal patterns traditional methods miss.
Understanding what drives box office success has practical implications beyond just making studios money. When studios make better investment decisions, they can take more creative risks rather than churning out safe franchise sequels. For audiences, improved decision-making could mean more diverse films getting greenlit. For data science, this demonstrates how machine learning can extract meaningful patterns from complex domains where art intersects with commerce.



The main objectives of this data collection phase were to:

Gather financial data (budget and revenue) for a large sample of theatrical releases
Collect cast and crew information to analyze the impact of talent on performance
Obtain genre classifications and temporal features to study market patterns
Ensure data quality by filtering for complete records and sufficient vote counts
Create a dataset suitable for exploratory analysis, clustering, and predictive modeling

By collecting this comprehensive data, I aimed to identify which factors most strongly predict profitability, whether different types of movies follow different patterns, and how release timing affects success rates.

title: Data Cleaning
text:
Data cleaning is the process of identifying and correcting quality issues in raw data to prepare it for analysis. The purpose of performing data cleaning on this dataset is to remove invalid records, handle missing information, and engineer features necessary for machine learning models.
The raw data from TMDB contained 2,812 movies, but several data quality issues made portions unsuitable for analysis. I identified unrealistic financial values, missing cast information, and statistical outliers requiring removal. Beyond addressing quality issues, I engineered five new features that didn’t exist in the raw data but are essential for profitability analysis.
The goal was to transform the raw dataset into a clean, analysis-ready format with complete records and meaningful features. The cleaning process involved validating financial data, filtering problematic records, and creating derived features like ROI, success categories, budget tiers, and seasonal indicators.
Below is an outline of the cleaning approach:


The raw dataset had several problems requiring attention:
Unrealistic Financial Values: Some movies showed budgets under $1 million or revenues under $1,000, likely representing data entry errors or incomplete records.
Statistical Outliers: A handful of records showed ROI values exceeding 100x, representing extreme outliers that would distort analysis.
Missing Information: Some records lacked complete cast or production company information needed for popularity-based analysis.





I created five new features before applying validation filters, ensuring derived metrics were available for filtering criteria.
ROI Calculation: I calculated return on investment by dividing revenue by budget, providing the primary profitability metric.
Binary Profitability: I created a binary indicator marking whether films earned more than they cost.
Success Categories: I classified films into four performance tiers (Bomb, Modest, Hit, Blockbuster) based on ROI thresholds.
Budget Tiers: I grouped films by production budget into four spending categories (Low, Medium, High, Blockbuster) reflecting industry breakpoints.
Release Seasons: I categorized release months into three seasonal periods (Fall, Holiday, Summer) reflecting industry release patterns.



I applied quality thresholds to remove problematic records while maintaining sufficient sample size.
Budget Threshold: Films with budgets below $1 million were excluded as these likely represent incomplete data rather than theatrical releases.
Revenue Threshold: Revenue below $1,000 indicated data quality issues and was filtered out.
ROI Threshold: ROI above 100x represented statistical outliers and was removed.
Completeness Requirement: Records missing cast or production company information were dropped as these features are required for analysis.

title: General Tips and Expectations
text:
Remember, slow and steady wins the race
Making steady, incremental progress on a large project generally makes it more manageable. Rushing to throw something together under a tight deadline often turns the process into a nightmare.



This is a graduate-level class, so each project should be viewed as specifications, not simple step-by-step requirements. Graduate-level work must be creative, individualized, and of high quality. To achieve an A-level grade, you are expected to exceed the specifications and create unique, novel solutions.
For example: If you’re asked to build visualizations to support your data science story, you won’t be told how many or what type of visualizations to create. This is up to you, based on your data and the creativity and quality you want to demonstrate.
We want you to move away from expecting someone else to tell you what to do, how to do it, and how much to do. Instead, you’ll adopt a professional approach—reviewing specifications provided in the assignments, determining what’s needed to exceed expectations, and demonstrating professional excellence.
There are countless ways to approach the project requirements, so be creative and thoughtful. Instructions outline the minimum requirements, but exceeding them will elevate the quality of your work.
Autonomy and Critical Thinking:

In the workplace, step-by-step instructions are rare. You’ll need to interpret broad requirements and deliver professional results. Producing high-quality, accurate work with limited guidance is a key professional skill.
At this stage, move away from asking, “Do I have to do XYZ?” Instead, critically analyze challenges. If something is unclear, investigate and break it down fundamentally.

Developing problem-solving skills is crucial. While it’s important to work independently for at least 10–20 minutes, if you’re still stuck after 30 minutes, seek help. Being resourceful is important, but knowing when to ask for assistance is equally valuable.



“Data science” is essentially a collection of useful computational and mathematical skills (statistics, cloud computing, machine learning, coding, etc). However, to maximize your effectiveness, these skills should be applied to a domain of interest (e.g., materials science, finance, healthcare, etc). Focusing and learning about a particular domain will help you specialize and make you more marketable.
That beind said, don’t worry about choosing the “perfect” domain—it’s always possible to pivot later, as many of the skills learned, such as problem-solving, critical thinking, and self-education, are transferable across all fields.



Impact in science refers to the significance and influence of research, often measured by metrics like citations, impact factor of journals, and indices like h-index. These metrics reflect how widely recognized and valuable the work is within the scientific community. Such quanities are used to compare researchers and journals, and are used to determine grant funding and career opportunities.

Impact Factor (IF):

A measure of a journal’s influence, calculated by averaging the number of citations to articles published in the journal over the past two years.
Higher impact factors indicate a more influential journal.

Number of Citations:

The total count of how often a researcher’s work is cited by others, reflecting its influence within the scientific community.
More citations generally signal broader recognition or relevance of the research.

h-index:

A metric that measures both productivity and citation impact. An h-index of 10 means a researcher has 10 papers each cited at least 10 times.
Higher h-index indicates more influential and widely recognized work.

i10-index:

Counts the number of a researcher’s publications with at least 10 citations.
A straightforward measure of citation impact, commonly used by Google Scholar.

Importance of Citations:

Citations indicate that other researchers find the work valuable for their own research, increasing its perceived credibility and impact in the field.

A metric that measures both productivity and citation impact. An h-index of 10 means a researcher has 10 papers each cited at least 10 times.
Higher h-index indicates more influential and widely recognized work.

i10-index:

Counts the number of a researcher’s publications with at least 10 citations.
A straightforward measure of citation impact, commonly used by Google Scholar.

Citations indicate that other researchers find the work valuable for their own research, increasing its perceived credibility and impact in the field.

title: Hollywood’s $100 Million Gamble: Can AI Predict Box Office Hits?
text:
Have you ever walked out of a movie theater thinking “that was incredible”? Or maybe left wondering how a studio greenlit something so awful it made you want a refund? If you’ve had either experience, you’re not alone. Hollywood invests billions in film production every year trying to capture that magic, yet predicting which movies will succeed remains incredibly difficult. You’d think an industry that’s survived over a century would have cracked the code by now.
Studios routinely bet $100+ million on productions with no guarantee anyone will show up, while low-budget indies shot for pennies occasionally become cultural phenomena. There has to be a pattern somewhere, right? This project digs into that question using machine learning to analyze 2,691 films from The Movie Database. The goal wasn’t just to build a prediction model, but to understand what actually separates the blockbusters from the box office bombs.
Turns out, machine learning can predict movie profitability with 77.7% accuracy using only information available before release: budget, cast popularity, genre, and release timing. More importantly, the analysis reveals patterns that challenge some common assumptions about what makes movies work. Bigger budgets don’t always mean better returns. A-list casts matter as much as production value. And timing a release can boost success probability by 14%.

title: Hollywood’s $100 Million Gamble: Can AI Predict Box Office Hits?
text:
Why This Matters
This isn’t just an academic exercise. Understanding what drives box office success has real implications for how studios allocate hundreds of millions of dollars, which films get made, and ultimately what ends up on our screens. When studios make better investment decisions, they can take more creative risks because they’re not betting the company on every tentpole.
For moviegoers, this matters too. If studios better understand what makes films successful, maybe we get more variety instead of the seventh Marvel sequel or fourth unnecessary reboot. Maybe mid-budget original films get greenlit more often. This analysis suggests they’re actually the sweet spot for returns.
Beyond the industry implications, this project demonstrates something broader about data science. Box office performance depends on complex interactions between art, commerce, timing, and culture. These factors don’t fit into neat formulas, yet machine learning can still extract meaningful patterns from the messiness. If we can predict movie success, what else that seems unpredictable might actually have hidden structure?

title: Hollywood’s $100 Million Gamble: Can AI Predict Box Office Hits?
text:
Research Questions
This analysis addresses five specific questions:

Can we actually predict movie profitability using only pre-release information? Not after marketing campaigns launch or opening weekend happens, but during production when decisions actually get made?
Which factors matter most? Everyone says budget and stars matter, but how much? Is there a hierarchy?
Does spending more always mean earning more? Or is there a budget sweet spot where returns peak?
Are there distinct “types” of successful movies? Do blockbusters, mid-budget films, and indies follow completely different playbooks?
How much does timing actually matter? We all know summer blockbusters exist, but can we quantify the advantage?

title: Hollywood’s $100 Million Gamble: Can AI Predict Box Office Hits?
text:
Literature Review
Here’s the thing about predicting box office success: people have been trying to crack this code for decades. Studios have always wanted to know which projects will print money and which will tank spectacularly. For most of Hollywood history, that came down to executive instinct, star power assessments, and looking at what worked last summer. But can data actually do better than gut feeling?

What the Research Says
Turns out, researchers have been asking the same question. Ahmed et al. analyzed over 2,000 movies to figure out what really matters1. They tested 50+ different features and landed on something interesting. Cast popularity was the single strongest predictor. Not budget, not genre, but whether audiences actually cared about who was in the movie. They also found that budgets have diminishing returns above $150M. Throwing more money at production doesn’t guarantee proportionally better results. Their Random Forest model hit 79% accuracy, which is pretty close to the 77.7% this analysis achieved. That consistency across different datasets suggests we might actually be approaching the real ceiling for how predictable movies can be.
The timing piece matters too. Ahmed’s research showed holiday and summer releases significantly outperform other periods1. Not shocking if you think about it. People have more free time, they’re in the mood to go out, and families are looking for activities. But quantifying that advantage helps studios make smarter release decisions rather than just following tradition. The advantage is substantial.
Kim et al. pushed things further by adding social media sentiment to the mix2. They scraped Twitter and review sites for 1,500 movies released between 2015-2019, feeding all that buzz into a deep learning model. The result? 82% accuracy. Better than Ahmed’s model, but not dramatically so. And here’s the catch: getting all that social media data requires real-time collection during marketing campaigns. You can’t predict success during pre-production if you need to wait for Twitter reactions to the first trailer. Still, their work revealed something useful. Genre matters for how sentiment plays. Negative buzz can actually help horror films because controversy drives ticket sales, while it kills romantic comedies. The relationship between marketing buzz and box office isn’t universal.
Li and Liu took a completely different angle3. Instead of predicting individual movies, they forecasted entire markets. How much will the US box office total next year? What about China? They used economic indicators like GDP and theater capacity, building Support Vector Machine models that proved surprisingly accurate. Their big takeaway: simpler models with fewer high-quality predictors often beat complex ones. You don’t need 50 features if you pick the right 5. They also validated something important for this project. Budget remains fundamental across every approach. Whether you’re predicting one movie or an entire market, production budget keeps showing up as critical.


The Industry Reality

Academic papers are great, but Hollywood operates in the real world where actual millions are on the line. The gap between theory and practice tells its own story.
Take Cinelytic, an analytics platform studios actually use. They claim 99% accuracy forecasting the US box office a year in advance by analyzing 19 key variables4. That’s way higher than academic benchmarks. Of course, their methodology is proprietary. They’re selling a service, not publishing research, and they have access to data academics don’t. Studio executives using Cinelytic know actual marketing budgets, theater commitments, and distributor relationships before films release. That granular information probably explains some of the accuracy gap.
But even with fancy prediction tools, Hollywood is struggling right now. Variety’s coverage of the 2025 box office paints a sobering picture5. Domestic revenues are projected at $9.3-9.5 billion compared to the $10.5-11 billion that used to be routine before COVID. Box office analyst Shawn Robbins calls this “the new normal” rather than continued recovery. The industry isn’t bouncing back. It’s stabilizing at a lower level.
The long-term outlook is even more concerning. PwC’s Global Entertainment & Media Outlook forecasts that box office won’t return to pre-COVID levels even by 20296. Full recovery might not happen until 2030. This isn’t just pandemic hangover. It’s structural change driven by streaming competition. As PwC analyst Bart Spiegel puts it, “While ticket prices are rising, admissions (volume) are not expected to return to pre-pandemic levels.” Studios are charging more per ticket to make up for fewer butts in seats. That’s not a growth strategy. That’s damage control.


The Forecasting Business
Professional box office forecasting has become its own industry, which tells you something about how valuable accurate predictions are. Firms like Gower Street Analytics and Box Office Theory provide subscription services to studios, exhibitors, and investors who need projections for planning7. Should we move this release date? How many theaters should we book? What marketing spend does this film justify? These aren’t academic questions. They’re multimillion-dollar decisions that need answers.
What’s interesting is that professional forecasters solve a different problem than academic researchers. Academics optimize for explainability and reproducibility across large datasets. They want models that make sense and can be validated. Industry forecasters optimize for accuracy on specific high-stakes decisions. They want the right answer for this particular movie releasing next month, even if the model is a black box. The goals diverge.
Gower Street CEO Dimitrios Mitsinikos describes tracking everything from GDP growth to the number of movie screens in each market to predict performance months in advance7. That level of detail goes way beyond what most academic models use. But it also makes the models less generalizable. A forecast optimized for the Chinese market in Q4 2025 might not teach us much about universal patterns in box office success.
The Numbers, a leading box office data aggregator, recently made a revealing change8. They redefined “wide release” from 600 theaters to 2,000 theaters. Why? Because getting a movie into 600 locations has become logistically trivial with digital distribution. The old threshold didn’t mean anything anymore. This seemingly technical adjustment actually reveals something about the industry. The middle ground between limited release and true wide release has expanded. Films playing in 600-1,999 theaters now occupy a space that didn’t really exist pre-pandemic, often using hybrid theatrical-streaming strategies that historical models never had to account for.


Bridging Research and Reality
So what do we actually know? Academic research and industry practice converge on a few core findings. Cast and budget matter most. Tree-based machine learning methods like Random Forest and Gradient Boosting consistently outperform traditional regression. Release timing creates measurable advantages. And prediction accuracy seems to plateau around 75-82% for academic models, though industry claims higher with proprietary data.
But here’s what’s changed. Most academic research uses data through 2019-2020. The world is different now. Streaming competition has intensified. Theatrical windows have shrunk from months to weeks. Marketing has shifted heavily toward social media and viral moments. International markets, especially China, have become less reliable for Hollywood product. And audience behavior has fundamentally shifted. People are pickier about what justifies a theater visit versus waiting for streaming.
This project bridges that gap by using current data that reflects post-pandemic reality. The 77.7% accuracy landing right in the established academic range suggests something important: the fundamental patterns remain stable even as the industry evolves. What changes isn’t whether cast and budget predict success. It’s the baseline success rate itself. Fewer movies succeed overall in the new landscape, but the factors determining which ones do remain consistent.
The cluster analysis adds something academic papers typically don’t provide. Instead of treating all films as equivalent and just predicting success or failure, the clustering reveals four distinct types of movies with completely different risk-return profiles. Blockbusters, mid-budget hits, standard indies, and breakout indies each follow different playbooks. Studios making $150M tentpoles face different challenges than producers shooting $5M indies. Recognizing those differences matters for practical decision-making.


What Data Can’t Predict
There’s a limit to all this, though. Data science can identify patterns in what usually works, but it can’t manufacture cultural phenomena. Nobody’s algorithm predicted “Barbenheimer,” where two totally unrelated films drove each other’s success through organic social media synergy9. Barbie and Oppenheimer created lightning in a bottle. Same with Paranormal Activity turning a $15,000 budget into $193M through word-of-mouth that couldn’t be engineered.
The best prediction models provide one input into decision-making, not the whole answer. As Variety’s analysis of the 2025 box office noted, studios need films that “start with a bang, end with a bang” to reengage global audiences5. Data can tell you which projects have that potential based on historical patterns. But it can’t tell you when to take a creative risk on something that breaks all the rules. Sometimes you need the algorithm. Sometimes you need to ignore it and trust your gut.
The real value isn’t replacing human judgment. It’s making that judgment more informed. When a studio executive looks at a script and thinks “this could be special,” prediction models can reality-check whether “special” translates to “profitable.” They can flag when a gut feeling aligns with historical patterns versus when it’s wishful thinking. That combination of intuition backed by data is probably more powerful than either alone.

text:
The two audiences
Knowing your audience in data science writing is crucial because it shapes how you present information. Technical stakeholders may require detailed explanations of methodologies, while non-technical audiences need clear, simplified insights and data-driven conclusions. Tailoring your message ensures your analysis is both understandable and impactful, driving informed decision-making.

Examples of technical audiences include data scientists, software engineers, and IT professionals. These individuals expect detailed explanations of models, algorithms, methodologies, or system architectures, and they’re comfortable with technical jargon, such as discussing hyperparameters, programming frameworks, or machine learning techniques.
Non-technical audiences include executives, marketing teams, and clients. They prioritize high-level insights, actionable results, and visualizations that convey the impact of data without requiring an understanding of complex methods. For instance, a CEO may want to know how a model affects business strategy or revenue, without diving into the underlying technical details.

In this project you will cater to both audiences. This is done by having regions of your website for both audiences (see website struture)

Graduate level work
This is a graduate-level class, so each project should be viewed as specifications, not simple step-by-step requirements. Graduate-level work must be creative, individualized, and of high quality. To achieve an A-level grade, you are expected to exceed the specifications and create unique, novel solutions.
For example: If you’re asked to build visualizations to support your data science story, you won’t be told how many or what type of visualizations to create. This is up to you, based on your data and the creativity and quality you want to demonstrate.
We want you to move away from expecting someone else to tell you what to do, how to do it, and how much to do. Instead, you’ll adopt a professional approach—reviewing specifications provided in the assignments, determining what’s needed to exceed expectations, and demonstrating professional excellence.
There are countless ways to approach the project requirements, so be creative and thoughtful. Instructions outline the minimum requirements, but exceeding them will elevate the quality of your work.
Autonomy and Critical Thinking:

In the workplace, step-by-step instructions are rare. You’ll need to interpret broad requirements and deliver professional results. Producing high-quality, accurate work with limited guidance is a key professional skill.
At this stage, move away from asking, “Do I have to do XYZ?” Instead, critically analyze challenges. If something is unclear, investigate and break it down fundamentally.

Developing problem-solving skills is crucial. While it’s important to work independently for at least 10–20 minutes, if you’re still stuck after 30 minutes, seek help. Being resourceful is important, but knowing when to ask for assistance is equally valuable.

The intersection of skills and domain knowledge
“Data science” is essentially a collection of useful computational and mathematical skills (statistics, cloud computing, machine learning, coding, etc). However, to maximize your effectiveness, these skills should be applied to a domain of interest (e.g., materials science, finance, healthcare, etc). Focusing and learning about a particular domain will help you specialize and make you more marketable.
That beind said, don’t worry about choosing the “perfect” domain—it’s always possible to pivot later, as many of the skills learned, such as problem-solving, critical thinking, and self-education, are transferable across all fields.

title: Project instruction:
text:
What is “impact”?
Impact in science refers to the significance and influence of research, often measured by metrics like citations, impact factor of journals, and indices like h-index. These metrics reflect how widely recognized and valuable the work is within the scientific community. Such quanities are used to compare researchers and journals, and are used to determine grant funding and career opportunities.

Impact Factor (IF):

A measure of a journal’s influence, calculated by averaging the number of citations to articles published in the journal over the past two years.
Higher impact factors indicate a more influential journal.

Number of Citations:

The total count of how often a researcher’s work is cited by others, reflecting its influence within the scientific community.
More citations generally signal broader recognition or relevance of the research.

h-index:

A metric that measures both productivity and citation impact. An h-index of 10 means a researcher has 10 papers each cited at least 10 times.
Higher h-index indicates more influential and widely recognized work.

i10-index:

Counts the number of a researcher’s publications with at least 10 citations.
A straightforward measure of citation impact, commonly used by Google Scholar.

Importance of Citations:

Citations indicate that other researchers find the work valuable for their own research, increasing its perceived credibility and impact in the field.

title: Project instruction:
section: What makes a good research project?
text:
What makes a good research project?
Professional academic or industrial research is all about discovery, improvement, and novelty. You don’t necessarily need to have a project that acheive the following, but here are some guidelines for what makes “high impact” projects:
In no particular order:

Novel computational tools: For example, development of a new Python package to tackle a class of problem which doesn’t have an existing suitable tool.
Creating more user-friendly tools: For example, there might be a great C++ code, but with no python analogue. Python is easier to use, so if you make a pythonic version of an existing tool, it may get higher adoption, provided it is more or less as efficient to the competitors.
More efficient tools or methods: Achieving something 1.25x, 2x, 10x or 10000x faster than existing methods, or creating a new code package that is more efficient than a previous one.
Novel methods: A completely new way of doing something (e.g. new classification algorithm)
Existing methods applied to new domains: Using established methods to solve problems in a novel domain, e.g. applying a particular classification methodology to a problem or dataset that no one has applied it to before. Extent of impact obviously depends on the importance of the domain or use-case.
Creation of novel Data Sets: Provides well-curated, clean datasets that can be used to address important scientific questions or problems.(often more useful if there is an accompanying API)
New insights or phenomena: Using data analysis techniques to uncover new insights or patterns that address key questions or problems. For example, discovering overarching governing rules (e.g., differential equations) that describe some observed phenomena.

Solves a Major Problem: Addresses a critical or unresolved issue in the field, offering a breakthrough or significant advancement.

Robust Data and Methodology: Employs sound, validated methodologies and high-quality data to ensure credibility and reliability (i.e. doing something rigorously, correctly, and generally better than the competition).
Interdisciplinary Impact: Influences multiple fields or areas of study, increasing the breadth of its significance.
High Citation Potential: Likely to be widely cited due to its significance, relevance, and applicability across different areas.

You can, of course, have multiple of these components in a single project, which will increase its prestige.
This is especially true when conducting academic research. Publications need to be novel and make a unique contribution to the body of human knowledge; otherwise, they will not be highly cited or considered particularly important.

title: Project instruction:
text:
Time management
80-20 Rule: This rule of thumb suggests that 80% of results come from 20% of causes. In other words, a small number of key factors drive the majority of outcomes. This principle applies to project management, where a few critical steps or decisions often determine the success of a project.
For example, it might take one week of steady work (30-40 hours) to complete 80% of a project, while the final 20% could take an additional four weeks.

Projects tend to expand to fill the time available. No creative project—whether a book, song, poem, or paper—is ever truly 100% complete. There is an asymptotic limit as \(t \rightarrow \infty\), and true perfection is unattainable. The key is knowing when to “call it done.” This might happen at 95% or 99% completion, but eventually, we all have to stop. Strive to take this project as far as possible, but remember to stop and “call it done” at some point.

text:
Visualization guidelines
Visualizations are a critical component of your portfolio. Use them strategically to support your narrative. The more visual representations of your data, the better—higher-quality visualizations will result in a higher grade. Ensure that all graphics follow best practices:

Choose the right chart type: Match the chart to the data (e.g., bar for categories, line for trends).
Maintain simplicity: Avoid clutter and focus on the essential message.
Use appropriate scales: Ensure axes have correct and intuitive scaling to avoid misinterpretation.
Label axes clearly: Include meaningful axis labels with units (e.g., “Temperature (°C)” or “Revenue (USD)”).
Include descriptive titles: Provide a concise, informative title that explains the visualization’s main takeaway.
Ensure consistency: Use uniform color schemes, fonts, and styles across all charts in a presentation.
Highlight key data: Use contrasting colors or annotations to draw attention to important points or trends.
Keep proportions accurate: Maintain correct data-to-visual size relationships to avoid distortion.
Consider the audience: Tailor the level of detail and style to the audience’s technical proficiency.
Test readability: Ensure fonts, colors, and elements are clear and legible in various formats and sizes.
Use interactivity carefully: Interactive features should add clarity, not complexity, to the visual.

Coding

Practice First
While not required, practice is highly beneficial. It’s also a good habit to write your code from scratch, as this will build your problem-solving skills. You can use the code provided by professors as a reference, but always strive to write your own. Starting with a blank page is a valuable practice.
To get comfortable with the methods, review and modify the R and Python codes provided in class. Try applying these to your project data and experiment with creating small toy datasets, such as a CSV file or a text corpus. This helps you understand the structure of the data and what the algorithms are doing.


Prototype and develop on a small data set
If you have big data, ALWAYS prototype on a small subset of the data, so that your code runs fast so that you can develop quickly, without waiting several minutes for each code cell to run. Do this by including a downsampling hyper-parameter at the beginning of your code, e.g. 0.1. When the code is robust and finalized, you can set the downsampling factor to 1, run it on the complete data set, and let your computer run overnight.
It is not a crazy idea to do a “trial run” of the project first from start to finish with a very basic dataset, e.g. penguins,diabetes, or iris. Make sure the “toy” data set is similar to your planned real world data set, for example, if you are planning an NLP project, don’t use a image dataset for your development process.

Clarifies Workflow: Understand the complete process from start to finish.

Quarto Includes
Quarto includes (e.g., {{< include _content.qmd >}}) are highly recommended for modularizing and organizing your content. While optional, they offer several advantages.
Note: You can include a .qmd file in a .ipynb file, but not vice versa.

Why Use Quarto Includes?

Modularization: Breaking your project into smaller, reusable chunks simplifies the management of complex documents. You can work on specific sections without altering the entire project.
Reusability: Includes allow you to reuse content blocks across multiple documents, making them ideal for repetitive sections like headers or footers.
Consistency: By using includes, you ensure uniformity across your documents. Updating an include file will automatically apply the changes wherever it’s used.
Simplifies Collaboration: In team settings, includes allow different contributors to work on separate sections simultaneously, reducing merge conflicts and making the project easier to maintain.
Improved Organization: Includes help keep your main files clean and focused by loading content from separate, well-organized files. This makes your project more manageable and easier to navigate.

title: Final Report
text:
Introduction
Hollywood operates on educated guesses. Studios bet hundreds of millions on films hoping audiences will show up, but nobody really knows which movies will succeed until they’re already in theaters. Executives rely on star power, looking at what worked last year, and gut instinct. But can data actually do better than that?
This project analyzed 2,691 films from The Movie Database to answer a specific question: can we predict whether a movie will be profitable using only information available before release? Not after trailers drop and social media starts buzzing, but back when the film is still in development and investment decisions need to be made. The features examined include production budget, cast popularity, genre, release timing, and runtime. All factors known months before opening weekend.
Machine learning classification models were trained to predict profitability, with Random Forest performing best at 77.7% accuracy. That means roughly 8 out of 10 times, the model correctly identified whether a film would make money. Beyond just prediction, the work reveals patterns about what actually drives box office success and whether different types of movies follow completely different playbooks. Turns out the answers challenge some conventional wisdom about how Hollywood works.



Key Findings
The exploratory data analysis revealed several patterns that matter for understanding box office success. Cast popularity and production budget emerged as co-dominant predictors, each contributing 25% of the model’s power. Not budget first with cast as a distant second. They tie. This quantifies what industry veterans know intuitively but challenges how studios actually allocate resources. The data says spending $150M on production while settling for cheaper talent is leaving money on the table.
High-budget films achieve near-optimal returns with lower risk. Films in the $80-150M range showed a median ROI of 2.9x, nearly matching Blockbusters at 3.1x while requiring half the capital investment. Budget and revenue correlate at 0.711, so spending more generally earns more, but the relationship isn’t linear. The $80-150M tier represents a strategic sweet spot: high enough to fund compelling production values, low enough to avoid the risk concentration of $150M+ tentpoles. Medium-budget films in the $20-80M range underperform at 2.3x ROI despite their popularity, suggesting this tier lacks the scale advantages of larger productions without gaining the efficiency benefits of smaller ones.
Release timing creates measurable advantages that studios can actually control. Holiday and Summer releases outperform Fall releases, with effects varying by genre. The data quantifies real advantages from strategic timing. Family films thrive during holidays, horror films peak in October, dramas compete better during awards season in fall, and action films dominate summer releases. This isn’t just tradition or superstition but measurable patterns in audience behavior.
The unsupervised learning phase revealed four natural movie archetypes with completely different risk-return profiles:

Blockbusters (13% of films): Require massive capital but deliver 97% success rates and 5.5x ROI
Mid-Budget Hits (35% of films): Balance risk and reward with 85% success and 4.2x ROI
Standard Indies (49% of films): Serve as volume plays with 61% success and 2.4x ROI
Breakout Indies (3% of films): Ultra-low-budget projects with 100% success and 39x ROI

This clustering matters because it shows different types of movies need fundamentally different strategies. A $150M tentpole faces different challenges than a $5M indie. Treating all films the same ignores real structural differences.
The supervised learning phase confirmed that prediction works but has limits. Random Forest achieved 77.7% accuracy, outperforming Logistic Regression at 75.3% and Gradient Boosting at 77.6%. More importantly, the model showed 96.3% recall, meaning it rarely misses profitable movies. For studios trying to avoid passing on the next Get Out, that high recall matters more than perfect overall accuracy. The 77.7% performance matches published academic research, which consistently achieves 75-82% regardless of method sophistication, suggesting a realistic ceiling for prediction given how many unpredictable factors influence movie success.
Genre analysis revealed substantial variation in success rates. Family films lead at 89% success, followed by Adventure at 85% and Fantasy at 84%. Animation and Action films both achieve roughly 80% success rates. At the lower end, Drama films succeed 71% of the time, while Thriller films face the toughest odds at 55% success.
This reflects audience appeal breadth rather than quality differences. Family content attracts multiple demographics and generates repeat viewings, while thrillers compete for narrower audiences. Genre also interacts with other factors in complex ways. Budget matters more for spectacle genres needing visual effects. Cast matters more for dramas and comedies relying on performance. Release timing effects vary by genre. No universal rules exist. Success factors depend on what type of film you’re making.
These findings highlight that box office success depends on interactions between multiple factors rather than any single variable. The patterns are strong enough to enable meaningful prediction but not deterministic. The 77.7% accuracy ceiling reflects irreducible uncertainty in creative industries where quality, cultural timing, and unpredictable word-of-mouth dynamics play crucial roles nobody can fully control.


Limitations
This project faced several limitations inherent to the data and methodology. The model predicts binary profitability rather than specific revenue amounts, so studios learn whether a film will likely make money but not whether it will earn $50M or $500M. Marketing quality represents a significant unmeasured variable. The analysis uses budget as a proxy for marketing spend but cannot account for campaign execution, where a brilliant campaign can save a mediocre film or a terrible campaign can sink a good one.
Cultural phenomena remain fundamentally unpredictable. No algorithm would have predicted “Barbenheimer” where Barbie and Oppenheimer drove each other’s success through organic social media synergy. These lightning-in-a-bottle moments reshape industries precisely because they’re unprecedented and can’t appear in historical patterns.
The temporal coverage poses challenges for applying findings to today’s market. Most data comes from before streaming competition intensified to current levels. Theatrical windows have shrunk from months to weeks, and audience behavior continues shifting toward selectivity about what justifies theater visits versus waiting for streaming. That said, the consistency of core predictors like cast and budget across time periods suggests fundamental patterns remain stable even as the industry evolves.

Finally, the 77.7% accuracy ceiling suggests inherent unpredictability in creative industries. Movies involve too many variables: creative quality, cultural timing, competitive landscape, marketing execution, word-of-mouth dynamics. Even with perfect data and optimal algorithms, some irreducible uncertainty remains. The convergence of multiple academic studies achieving similar accuracy regardless of method sophistication suggests this represents a realistic limit rather than a methodological failure.


Future Research
Several directions could extend this work beyond its current scope. Incorporating social media sentiment analysis during marketing campaigns would capture buzz momentum that pre-production data misses. Research by Kim et al. achieved 82% accuracy by adding Twitter and review site sentiment to traditional features. Adding competitive landscape analysis would account for what else releases the same weekend, since a good movie facing Avengers has different prospects than one with a clear field.
Including filmmaker track records as quantifiable features could improve predictions. Some directors and producers consistently deliver: Christopher Nolan, James Cameron, Jordan Peele. Their involvement changes risk profiles in ways executives recognize but the model currently ignores. Building genre-specific models might increase accuracy by capturing nuances a universal model misses, since horror and family films follow different rules.
Expanding to revenue regression rather than binary classification would provide more actionable guidance. Instead of “probably profitable,” studios want “probably $150-200M domestic.” This requires different modeling approaches, additional features like screen count and international data, and handling the long tail of revenue distributions.
These extensions would likely require access to proprietary industry data on marketing spends, theater bookings, and competitive positioning that aren’t publicly available. Partnerships with studios or distributors could enable research bridging the gap between academic models and industry practice.


Conclusion
This project demonstrates that box office success is predictable to a meaningful degree using machine learning, but not perfectly so. The 77.7% accuracy achieved matches academic benchmarks and likely represents a realistic ceiling given the inherent unpredictability of creative industries. The analysis confirms that cast popularity and budget matter equally, mid-budget films offer optimal risk-adjusted returns, and strategic release timing creates measurable advantages.
The identification of four distinct movie archetypes provides practical insight beyond simple prediction. Studios making $150M tentpoles face different challenges than producers shooting $5M indies. Recognizing these differences enables tailored strategies rather than universal rules that fit nobody well. The high recall at 96.3% means the model rarely misses profitable opportunities, which matters more for practical decision-making than perfect overall accuracy.
While data-driven approaches improve investment decisions at the margins, they won’t replace creative judgment. Cultural phenomena like “Barbenheimer” remain unpredictable by definition. The real value lies in combining algorithmic pattern recognition with human intuition. When executives evaluate projects, prediction models can reality-check whether gut feelings align with historical patterns or represent wishful thinking.
The post-pandemic landscape has introduced new complexities: streaming competition, shrinking theatrical windows, shifting audience behavior. Yet the fundamental predictors remain consistent across time periods. What changes isn’t whether cast and budget matter but the baseline success rate. Fewer movies succeed overall in the new normal, but the factors determining which ones do stay stable. This suggests the patterns identified here will remain relevant even as the industry continues evolving.
Future research incorporating social media sentiment, competitive landscape, and filmmaker track records could push accuracy higher. But even at current levels, these models provide actionable intelligence for an industry that has traditionally relied on instinct. The studios that combine creative vision with data-driven decision-making will consistently outperform those depending on either alone. That’s not speculation. It’s what the data shows.

title: Methods
text:
All data used in this project comes from The Movie Database (TMDB) API. TMDB maintains one of the largest databases of movie information with reliable financial data, cast details, and production metadata. The API provides free access for research purposes with reasonable rate limits.
I used automated API queries with Python’s requests library to systematically retrieve movie lists and detailed information for each film, filtering for records with complete budget and revenue data.



I selected TMDB for several reasons. The API provides comprehensive movie data including financial information that many other sources don’t make publicly available. TMDB’s data quality is reliable, maintained by a large community of contributors. The API documentation is clear and the rate limits are reasonable for academic research. Most importantly, TMDB includes both recent releases and historical films, enabling analysis across different eras of cinema.



The collection process used two TMDB API endpoints. The /discover/movie endpoint retrieved lists of popular movies sorted by popularity with vote counts of at least 100. The /movie/{id} endpoint provided detailed information for each film including cast, crew, and financial data. I only retained movies with non-zero budget and revenue values since these are required for profitability analysis.


Discovery Endpoint: /discover/movie - Sorted by popularity (sort_by='popularity.desc') - Filtered for vote count (vote_count.gte=100) - Retrieved paginated lists of movies
Details Endpoint: /movie/{id}
- Appended credits data (append_to_response='credits') - Retrieved comprehensive movie information including financials



I implemented a 0.25-second delay between requests to respect API rate limits and avoid overloading TMDB servers. This results in approximately 4 requests per second, well within acceptable usage. The collection process took several hours but ensured ethical API usage.




I extracted 18 features from API responses:
Financial Metrics: - Budget (production cost in USD) - Revenue (box office earnings in USD)
Cast and Crew: - Top 5 cast members by billing order - Average cast popularity (aggregated from individual actor popularity scores) - Director name
Production Details: - Up to 3 production companies
- All genres (pipe-separated string) - Primary genre (first listed)
Film Metadata: - Title, movie ID, release date - Runtime (minutes) - Vote average and vote count (user ratings from TMDB) - Popularity score (TMDB metric) - Overview text (first 500 characters)
Temporal Features: - Release year (extracted from release date) - Release month (extracted from release date)



I stored the collected data in tabular format with each row representing one movie and each column representing a feature. Multi-value fields like genres and cast were stored as pipe-separated strings (e.g., “Action|Adventure|Sci-Fi”) to maintain a flat table structure while preserving all information. This format facilitates easy loading into pandas DataFrames for subsequent analysis.

title: Exploratory Data Analysis
text:
Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) is the process of examining and visualizing data to understand its characteristics, identify patterns, and uncover relationships between variables. The purpose of performing EDA on this data is to gain deeper insights into what drives box office success and to prepare the dataset for machine learning modeling.
I conducted univariate, bivariate, and multivariate analyses to examine the cleaned dataset of 2,691 movies. The analysis explored distributions of key variables (budget, revenue, ROI), relationships between features (budget-revenue correlation, genre patterns, seasonal effects), and patterns that inform the prediction task.
The goal was to answer exploratory questions: How does budget relate to revenue? Do certain genres perform better? Does release timing matter? What’s the typical ROI distribution? These insights shaped feature selection and informed expectations for model performance.
Below is an outline of the analytical approach:


The cleaned dataset contains 2,691 movies with 23 features spanning financial metrics, cast information, genre classifications, and temporal characteristics. Key variables include:
Financial Variables: Budget, revenue, ROI, profitability (binary), success category (4-class)
Cast and Production: Cast popularity, production companies, director
Genre and Classification: Primary genre, all genres, budget tier
Temporal Features: Release date, release year, release month, release season
Film Characteristics: Runtime, vote average, vote count, popularity score





I examined the distribution of individual variables to understand their characteristics and identify potential issues.
Numerical Variables: I generated summary statistics (mean, median, standard deviation) and visualized distributions using histograms. This revealed the range and spread of budget, revenue, and ROI values.
Categorical Variables: I calculated frequency counts for genres, budget tiers, and seasons, visualizing them with bar charts to understand category balance.



I analyzed relationships between pairs of variables to identify patterns and correlations.
Budget-Revenue Relationship: I created scatter plots and calculated correlation coefficients to quantify the relationship between production spending and box office earnings.
Genre Performance: I compared success rates across genres using grouped bar charts to identify which categories perform best.
Seasonal Patterns: I analyzed profitability rates by release season to determine whether timing affects outcomes.



I examined interactions between multiple variables simultaneously.
Correlation Matrix: I generated a correlation heatmap showing relationships among all numerical features to identify multicollinearity and feature importance patterns.
Budget Tier Analysis: I compared ROI distributions across budget tiers using box plots to understand how spending level affects returns.

title: Unsupervised Learning
text:
Unsupervised learning is a type of machine learning that aims to discover hidden patterns and structure in data without labeled outcomes. The purpose of performing unsupervised learning on this data is to identify natural groupings of movies and understand whether different types of films follow distinct patterns in terms of budget, cast popularity, and box office performance.
I applied two main unsupervised learning techniques: dimensionality reduction for visualization and clustering for pattern discovery. For dimensionality reduction, I used Principal Component Analysis (PCA) to reduce the feature space while preserving variance. For clustering, I applied K-Means clustering to identify distinct movie archetypes based on their characteristics.
The goal was to determine whether movies naturally group into categories beyond simple genre classifications, and whether these groupings reveal insights about different risk-return profiles in the film industry.
Below is an outline of general information applied to all methods:


In order to be used in unsupervised learning, the data required preprocessing to ensure all features contributed equally to pattern detection.
Feature Selection - I selected numerical features that characterize movie production and performance: budget, revenue, cast popularity, runtime, and ROI. Categorical variables were excluded from clustering since K-Means requires numerical data.
Standardization - The data was scaled using Scikit-learn’s StandardScaler. This z-score standardization is critical for unsupervised learning since clustering algorithms are sensitive to feature magnitudes. Without scaling, budget (in millions) would dominate patterns over features like runtime (in minutes).
Handling Outliers - Extreme outliers were retained since they may represent legitimate movie archetypes (ultra-low-budget breakouts or massive tentpoles) rather than data errors.





Principal Component Analysis (PCA) reduces the dimensionality of data by transforming features into orthogonal principal components that capture maximum variance. PCA identifies linear combinations of original features that explain the most variation in the data.
I applied PCA to visualize the movie dataset in two dimensions while preserving as much information as possible. The first two principal components captured the most important patterns of variation across budget, revenue, cast popularity, and other features.
Purpose: PCA enables visualization of high-dimensional data and can reveal whether movies naturally separate into distinct groups based on their characteristics.



K-Means is a clustering algorithm that partitions data into k distinct groups by minimizing within-cluster variance. The algorithm iteratively assigns data points to clusters and updates cluster centers until convergence.
I applied K-Means clustering to identify natural groupings of movies. The algorithm groups films with similar characteristics (budget levels, cast popularity, revenue performance) into the same cluster.
Model Selection: I used the elbow method and silhouette analysis to determine the optimal number of clusters. The elbow method plots within-cluster sum of squares (WCSS) against k values, looking for the “elbow” where adding more clusters provides diminishing returns. Silhouette analysis measures how well each point fits within its assigned cluster.
Purpose: K-Means reveals whether movies fall into distinct categories with different production strategies and financial outcomes, beyond traditional genre classifications.

title: Data Collection
text:
The goal of this data collection phase was to gather comprehensive movie information from The Movie Database (TMDB) to analyze patterns in box office success. TMDB provides detailed financial data, cast information, production details, and temporal features needed for profitability analysis.

Executives rely on star power, comparable film analysis, and gut instinct, but data-driven approaches may reveal patterns traditional methods miss.

When studios make better investment decisions, they can take more creative risks rather than churning out safe franchise sequels. For audiences, improved decision-making could mean more diverse films getting greenlit. For data science, this demonstrates how machine learning can extract meaningful patterns from complex domains where art intersects with commerce.

Gather financial data (budget and revenue) for a large sample of theatrical releases
Collect cast and crew information to analyze the impact of talent on performance
Obtain genre classifications and temporal features to study market patterns
Ensure data quality by filtering for complete records and sufficient vote counts
Create a dataset suitable for exploratory analysis, clustering, and predictive modeling

By collecting this comprehensive data, I aimed to identify which factors most strongly predict profitability, whether different types of movies follow different patterns, and how release timing affects success rates.
